Do you think that mathematics (which we rely on for physics, chemistry, etc) are the "ultimate truth"? And at its core, are mathematics just our way of quantifying patterns in nature?
I've often pondered this same thing. You've put this idea in words better than I could of. I'll be waiting for some higher intelligence to come along and maybe actually provide some insight.

I think I can actually give you a pretty fair answer to that, but it'll take a minute. Bear with me.

A 'scientific model' is a way of describing something. Models are not intended to capture the whole truth about the things in question, they are just intended as a useful and simplified way of describing a part of it. Everybody knows they are not really true, but they can still be quite useful.

For example, you can model gravity as an attractive force, like magnetism. The model works quite well for most purposes, even though it's more accurate to say that gravity is a result of warping spacetime. The model is still useful, despite not really being true.

I believe that all of our understandings are necessarily just models like this. We don't, and can't, really know the full truth about anything. We lack the context to even begin. All we can do is to model what we see in a useful way, and as our models become better our predictive and prescriptive power grows; we can use this power to walk on the moon, but we do this without any real grasp of the truth. What we call truth is a just model that works within the parameters that matter to us, and we know that the next new discovery will change the model yet again.

Math provides the basis for most of our really useful models. It, like the models themselves, is a utility, not a truth. Every mathematical system is based upon arbitrary assumptions, none are complete in and of themselves.

If you want to pray, pray to anything you like. If you want to make good predictions, or figure out how to achieve a certain result, find the best model and apply it correctly. If you want truth, you'll have to wait until you are no longer limited by human perception. But of course that's just one guy's opinion.
What are your thoughts on truth vs accuracy?

Well, like I said, a good model will give you predictive and/or prescriptive power. It will allow you to say things like, "I bet that bridge will break if you put a 20 ton truck on it" and "If you build the bridge this way instead of that way, your 20 ton truck will be OK".

I assume that this power is what you mean by accuracy. It means that within the limits and scope of the model, that the model is useful.

My belief - and I appreciate that it's just a belief, and article of faith rather than something that I can prove - is that reality, whatever it is, is not likely to be something that our human brains can ever comprehend. We don't expect a cat to comprehend metallurgy or a fish to comprehend a nuclear submarine - they just can't - because their brains are of limited power and were never adapted for grasping concepts like that. Our brains are similarly constrained for exactly the same reasons. We might be a million times smarter than the average cat, but there's no reason to think that the fundamental construction of the universe would happen to be accessible to our particular way of conceiving things. We, like our animal friends, were evolved for a very different purpose. We can grasp only that small, highly abstracted fraction of reality which we need to grasp.

Those who disagree may argue that our brains are advanced to a point where they can function as general-purpose learning machines that can tackle any problem. They see a progressive march towards finding truth, an ever-greater refinement with no limit in sight. I admit they might be correct, but I do not believe it. Our brains seem limitless only because we are trapped inside them. We can't comprehend what we can't comprehend. Neither can my cat. She just has no idea what she's missing, and she never will.

I'm not particularly convinced that there's even a truth to be discovered. You could finish this sentence, wake up in your bed and realize this whole conversation was a dream. You'd forget most of it upon waking and never give it a second thought. Our minds depend on an unchanging context, on the reliability of memory, on the world we wake up in today being the same world in which we awoke yesterday. That might not be a safe assumption. We have no idea what consciousness even is. It's very hard to describe an unchanging truth if we are unreliable narrators to ourselves.

Math is objective, our experience of reality is subjective. Our interpretation of reality using math is somewhere in between. I see red as I see red, you might not see the exact shade I see, but we can agree the numerical representation aka wavelength defines red. Que Sera, Sera.
